note: Curated atlas of notable figures, pinned at their birthplace. Coordinates are approximate to the town or district of birth. Blurbs are written for this site; the panel also pulls a live summary from Wikipedia when a visitor is online.

people.name: Albert Jackson
people.blurb: Born into slavery in Delaware and carried north to Toronto by his mother on the Underground Railroad. In 1882 he became Toronto's first Black letter carrier, and kept the post only because his community refused to let prejudice take it from him.

people.name: Ann Maria Jackson
people.blurb: Albert Jackson's mother. After two of her eldest children were sold and her husband died in a poorhouse, she learned four more were about to be sold and fled in November 1858 with the seven still with her, by way of Wilmington, Philadelphia and St. Catharines to Toronto. Escaping with seven children was almost unheard of.

people.name: Harriet Tubman
people.blurb: Escaped slavery and then returned again and again as a conductor on the Underground Railroad, leading dozens of people to freedom. She later scouted and spied for the Union Army.

people.name: Frederick Douglass
people.blurb: Taught himself to read in bondage, escaped north, and became the most commanding orator and writer of the American abolitionist movement.

people.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
people.blurb: Baptist minister who led the American civil rights movement through nonviolent mass action, from the Montgomery bus boycott to the march on Washington.

people.name: Rosa Parks
people.blurb: A seasoned organiser long before the day she would not give up her seat. Her refusal in Montgomery in 1955 set off a bus boycott that ran for over a year.

people.name: Viola Desmond
people.blurb: Nova Scotia businesswoman who refused to leave the whites-only floor of a New Glasgow cinema in 1946. Her fight against segregation now looks out from the Canadian ten dollar note.

people.name: Nelson Mandela
people.blurb: Spent twenty-seven years in prison for opposing apartheid, then walked out and led South Africa's negotiated turn to democracy as its first freely elected president.

people.name: Malala Yousafzai
people.blurb: Campaigned for girls' schooling in the Swat Valley as a child, survived being shot for it, and became the youngest person ever awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

people.name: Sitting Bull
people.blurb: Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man who united the Plains nations against the seizure of their lands and led them at the Little Bighorn.

people.name: Eddie Mabo
people.blurb: Meriam man whose decade-long case overturned the legal fiction of terra nullius and established Indigenous native title in Australian law.

people.name: Whina Cooper
people.blurb: Māori leader who at seventy-nine walked the length of the North Island at the head of the 1975 land march, carrying the call not one more acre.

people.name: Wangari Maathai
people.blurb: Founded the Green Belt Movement, which planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya while organising rural women against deforestation and misrule.

people.name: Sophie Scholl
people.blurb: Student in the White Rose resistance circle, executed at twenty-one for distributing leaflets against the Nazi regime in Munich.

people.name: Anne Frank
people.blurb: Kept a diary in a hidden annexe in Amsterdam for two years before her family was betrayed. Her writing became the most widely read personal account of the Holocaust.

people.name: Emmeline Pankhurst
people.blurb: Led the militant wing of the British suffrage movement, enduring repeated imprisonment and hunger strikes in the campaign for women's votes.

people.name: Marie Curie
people.blurb: Discovered polonium and radium, coined the term radioactivity, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

people.name: Ada Lovelace
people.blurb: Writing about Babbage's Analytical Engine, she saw that a machine might manipulate symbols rather than only numbers, and published what is read as the first algorithm.

people.name: Alan Turing
people.blurb: Laid the mathematical foundations of computing, broke German naval ciphers at Bletchley Park, and was prosecuted by the country he had helped save.

people.name: Rosalind Franklin
people.blurb: Her X-ray diffraction images of DNA, above all Photograph 51, made the double helix visible. She died at thirty-seven, before the Nobel was awarded for it.

people.name: Albert Einstein
people.blurb: Rewrote the physics of space, time, gravity and light. His 1905 papers alone reshaped four separate fields in a single year.

people.name: Nikola Tesla
people.blurb: Engineer whose alternating current system won the argument over how to electrify the world, alongside work on radio, motors and wireless power.

people.name: Katherine Johnson
people.place: White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, United States
people.blurb: NASA mathematician whose orbital calculations carried American astronauts into space and back. John Glenn would not fly until she had checked the numbers herself.

people.name: Tu Youyou
people.blurb: Searched classical Chinese medical texts for a malaria treatment and isolated artemisinin, a drug credited with saving millions of lives.

people.name: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
people.blurb: Physician and philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age whose Canon of Medicine was the standard medical reference from Samarkand to Paris for six centuries.

people.name: Al-Khwarizmi
people.blurb: Scholar of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad. Algebra takes its name from his book, and the word algorithm takes its name from his.

people.name: Leonardo da Vinci
people.blurb: Painter of the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper, and a notebook-filling anatomist, engineer and observer who treated art and science as one discipline.

people.name: Vincent van Gogh
people.blurb: Painted some nine hundred canvases in a decade and sold almost none in his lifetime. His colour and brushwork changed what European painting could do.

people.name: Frida Kahlo
people.blurb: Turned chronic pain, Mexican folk tradition and her own face into a body of self-portraits unlike anything else in twentieth century art.

people.name: Katsushika Hokusai
people.blurb: Printmaker of Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, including the Great Wave. His work reached Europe and reshaped Impressionism from a distance.

people.name: Emily Carr
people.blurb: Painted the forests and Indigenous villages of the Pacific Northwest coast, and took up writing in her sixties with equal force.

people.name: Albert Namatjira
people.blurb: Western Arrernte painter whose watercolours of the central Australian ranges made him famous nationally while the law still denied him ordinary rights.

people.name: Murasaki Shikibu
people.blurb: Lady-in-waiting at the Heian court and author of The Tale of Genji, widely held to be the world's first novel.

people.name: Jane Austen
people.blurb: Six novels of English provincial life whose irony and social precision have never gone out of print or out of argument.

people.name: Chinua Achebe
people.blurb: Things Fall Apart told the story of colonial arrival from the inside and is often called the founding work of modern African literature.

people.name: Rabindranath Tagore
people.blurb: Poet, composer and educator, the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. He wrote the national anthems of two countries.

people.name: Gabriel García Márquez
people.blurb: One Hundred Years of Solitude carried the imagined town of Macondo, and Latin American magical realism, around the world.

people.name: Jorge Luis Borges
people.blurb: Wrote short fictions about labyrinths, infinite libraries and forking time that quietly rearranged what a story could be.

people.name: Pablo Neruda
people.blurb: Chilean poet and diplomat whose range ran from love poems read by heart across a continent to the sweeping history of Canto General.

people.name: Maya Angelou
people.blurb: Poet and memoirist whose I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings opened a new kind of autobiography, alongside a life of civil rights work.

people.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
people.blurb: Carried music from the classical era into the romantic and wrote his late masterpieces, the Ninth Symphony among them, while profoundly deaf.

people.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
people.blurb: Composed from the age of five and left more than six hundred works by thirty-five, across opera, symphony, concerto and chamber music.

people.name: Antonio Vivaldi
people.blurb: Priest, violinist and teacher at a Venetian orphanage, where he wrote hundreds of concertos including The Four Seasons.

people.name: Miriam Makeba
people.blurb: Mama Africa. Her singing carried South African music worldwide and her testimony against apartheid cost her the right to return home for thirty years.

people.name: Fela Kuti
people.blurb: Invented Afrobeat out of highlife, jazz and funk, and used it as a platform against Nigeria's military governments at considerable personal cost.

people.name: Youssou N'Dour
people.blurb: Senegalese singer who took mbalax from Dakar's clubs to the world's stages, and later served as his country's minister of culture.

people.name: Louis Armstrong
people.blurb: Trumpeter and singer who moved jazz from ensemble music to the art of the soloist, and remained its most recognisable voice for fifty years.

people.name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
people.blurb: Developed satyagraha, nonviolent mass resistance, first in South Africa and then against British rule in India. His methods shaped movements on every continent.

people.name: Kwame Nkrumah
people.blurb: Led Ghana to independence in 1957, the first sub-Saharan colony to break free, and argued for a united Africa for the rest of his life.

people.name: Simón Bolívar
people.blurb: Led the campaigns that freed six South American nations from Spanish rule, and died disillusioned by the fragmentation that followed.

people.name: Sun Yat-sen
people.blurb: Central figure in the overthrow of China's last dynasty and the founding of its first republic, honoured on both sides of the Taiwan Strait.

people.name: Haile Selassie
people.blurb: Emperor of Ethiopia whose 1936 appeal to the League of Nations against invasion became one of the century's defining speeches.

people.name: Eva Perón
people.place: Los Toldos, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
people.blurb: Rose from rural poverty to become Argentina's first lady, campaigning for women's suffrage and labour rights before her death at thirty-three.

people.name: Saladin
people.blurb: Founded the Ayyubid dynasty and retook Jerusalem in 1187. Even his opponents in the Crusades wrote of his restraint towards the defeated.

people.name: Cleopatra VII
people.blurb: Last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, a formidable linguist and negotiator who held her kingdom's independence against Rome for two decades.

people.name: Genghis Khan
people.blurb: United the Mongol tribes and built the largest contiguous land empire in history, reopening trade and exchange across the whole of Eurasia.

people.name: Confucius
people.blurb: Teacher whose sayings on duty, learning and right conduct became the organising ethic of Chinese public life for more than two thousand years.

people.name: Jalal al-Din Rumi
people.blurb: Persian poet and Sufi mystic whose verse on longing and union is still among the most widely read poetry on earth.

people.name: Hypatia
people.blurb: Mathematician, astronomer and head of the Neoplatonist school at Alexandria, murdered by a mob in a season of religious violence.

people.name: Fatima al-Fihri
people.blurb: Founded the mosque and teaching institution at Fez in 859 that UNESCO recognises as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.

people.name: Ibn Battuta
people.blurb: Travelled roughly 120,000 kilometres over thirty years, from West Africa to China, and dictated an account that remains a window onto the fourteenth century world.

people.name: Zheng He
people.blurb: Ming admiral who led seven treasure fleet voyages across the Indian Ocean to Arabia and East Africa, decades before the European age of sail.

people.name: Edmund Hillary
people.blurb: With Tenzing Norgay, the first confirmed to reach the summit of Everest in 1953. He spent much of the rest of his life building schools and clinics in Nepal.

people.name: Tenzing Norgay
people.blurb: Sherpa mountaineer who reached the summit of Everest alongside Edmund Hillary, and always declined to say which of them stepped up first.

people.name: Pelé
people.blurb: Won three World Cups with Brazil, the only player ever to do so, and became football's first genuinely global figure.

people.name: Jackie Robinson
people.blurb: Broke the colour line in Major League Baseball in 1947, absorbing sustained abuse under an agreement not to answer it, and won Rookie of the Year.

people.name: Terry Fox
people.blurb: Ran a marathon a day across Canada on one leg and one prosthesis to raise money for cancer research, covering 5,373 kilometres before the disease stopped him.

people.name: Muhammad Ali
people.blurb: Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title and his prime years rather than be drafted to a war he opposed, and won that argument too.
